prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints tie credit limits to asset prices, so that small shocks are amplified and propagated into persistent economic fluctuations

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: a single part for Kiyotaki and Moore (B040). Asked which common criterion I rank first, my answer is clarity of attribution combined with conceptual generality, with maturity as the check on both. Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) isolate one mechanism. Borrowing limited by collateral value makes credit limits and asset prices feed on each other, so small shocks become large and persistent. The originating paper has two authors, and every B040 proposal in the files names the same pair. After nearly three decades the mechanism has been extended, criticised and built into the macro and policy models used after 2008. It is also used in corporate finance, where collateral and financing constraints shape investment. I count that as breadth of use, not as extra merit. I considered a two-part configuration. Adding one B044 name to the Kiyotaki-Moore pair would break up a jointly authored body of work and credit one person for a fragment, so I reject it. I have not found a second shortlisted part that meets B040's standard on both maturity and attribution. Round 1 moved one view of mine. If B044 is chosen, the trade-shock core should be Autor, Dorn and Hanson, not the Autor-Hanson pair I proposed in the opening. Krusell, Hjalmarsson and Teorell are right that Dorn co-authored the central papers, and I now treat the pair as a misattribution. This does not change my first choice. I also say plainly that the four-four split between B040 and B044 is not evidence of merit, and I am not trying to build consensus for its own sake.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises is the most serious reservation. I think it is narrower than it appears, because the 2022 work concerned intermediaries and bank runs while Kiyotaki-Moore concerns collateral values and asset prices in the real economy. But that is my judgement, and the committee has not verified it here. Second, direct empirical identification of the amplification mechanism is indirect, and its quantitative size in macro models is contested. Firm-level evidence supports the collateral channel in corporate investment (for example Chaney, Sraer and Thesmar on real-estate collateral, which I cite from general knowledge without verification). That supports the channel but does not settle how much aggregate amplification it produces. Third, a two-person award leaves out Gertler and Gilchrist, so it honours the mechanism over the more empirical and quantitative accelerator strand. Fourth, the case rests on one seminal paper and its extensions, and that is narrower than the broader empirical programmes in B044 and B002. If the committee finds the 2022 overlap substantive, or weights direct identification over conceptual generality, B044 narrowed to the trade-shock evidence would be the stronger choice.

responses.point: Krusell now prefers B044 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson, anchored on the trade-shock evidence. He grants that Kiyotaki-Moore has the cleanest attribution and about thirty years of use. He places it behind B044 because its empirical test is more indirect and the 2022 prize narrows its marginal novelty.
responses.response: I agree that indirect empirical testing is the main weakness of B040, and I list it among my own reservations. Two distinctions answer part of it. First, the collateral channel has been tested in firm-level investment data. That is relevant to a corporate-finance reader, though it does not establish the size of aggregate amplification. The citation should therefore credit the mechanism and its influence on how crises are modelled, not a measured magnitude. Second, a narrower, trade-shock-only citation does improve B044's attribution, and it answers my earlier objection that the task and trade strands blur together. I accept that and now name Dorn. Even so, I do not think direct identification outweighs conceptual generality, and B044 is still a decade younger, with shift-share inference and the size and persistence of effects still disputed. I treat the 2022 overlap as a question of mechanism. The earlier prize concerned bank runs and deposit insurance, and I do not see it as covering collateral-driven feedback between asset prices and credit limits.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B044 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He answers my round-1 question by arguing that one shared labour-demand question can hold the task framework and the trade-shock evidence in a single prize. He also calls this the main unresolved issue for B044. He lists B040 as an alternative for its cleaner attribution.
responses.response: I appreciate that he calls the one-prize-or-two question a judgement and not a settled fact. For me that open question is a cost, because it makes the credited set depend on how the committee frames the achievement. His own citation already narrows to the local-labour-market evidence and says it should not claim the whole technology-and-inequality literature. That is the right instinct and would be my condition for supporting B044 at all. Once the task lineage (Katz, Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu) is placed outside the citation, B044 becomes a trade-shock prize, which is a coherent but narrower claim than the one in his statement. I agree with him that the 2024 institutions prize does not make a China-shock award impossible. It is a different mechanism and a different object of identification. The remaining gap between us is maturity and conceptual weight, which I weigh in B040's favour.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, prefers B040 with the two originators. He qualified his opening wording: Gertler and Gilchrist should be excluded because the collateral-constraint mechanism is distinct and independently originated, not because the accelerator was already recognised. He keeps B044 with Autor and Hanson as his alternative and says indirect validation is common to foundational macro mechanisms.
responses.response: I agree with his corrected basis for excluding Gertler and Gilchrist, and I withdraw any reliance on prior recognition in my own case. Only Bernanke among the accelerator authors is a laureate, and he was recognised for the 2022 work on banks and crises. The exclusion is defensible only as a statement about where the originating mechanism lies, and I would say so openly with Dreber-Almenberg's point that this honours theory over tested evidence. I disagree with him on one matter. His alternative of Autor and Hanson alone leaves out a co-author of the central trade-shock papers, so I would use Autor, Dorn and Hanson if B044 is taken up. I also note that the chair and I are both B040 supporters, he in the same broad field. Our agreement is not independent evidence of merit, and I do not treat it as one.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B036 with Helpman and Melitz but names B040 as his main alternative and concedes that its attribution is cleaner. He argues that Melitz-style selection and reallocation is a distinct mechanism from the increasing-returns trade theory recognised in 2008. He also names the omitted Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as the strongest reservation against B036.
responses.response: I agree with his distinction from the 2008 prize. Within-industry selection and reallocation, tested on firm microdata, is a different discovery from representative-firm increasing returns, and I keep B036 as an alternative for that reason. The omitted co-originators are the difficulty. His point that explaining firm-level facts is a larger contribution than documenting them is reasonable, but it does not remove the boundary problem under a three-name cap. That is why I place B036 behind B040 on attribution, not on scientific quality. My view of B036 is closer to his than my ranking suggests, and I would not oppose it if the committee judged the attribution settled. His acceptance of B040's cleaner attribution is, for me, a point about attribution only. He does not claim that it outweighs the case for B036, and I do not read it as support.

uncertainties: How far the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, and Bernanke's earlier recognition on the financial accelerator, reduce B040's marginal case. My view that the mechanisms differ is a judgement, not a verified finding.

How much weight indirect empirical validation should carry against conceptual generality and a long record of use. The quantitative amplification effect is not settled, and the citation should not claim otherwise.
Whether leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist, whose work is the more empirical and quantitative strand, makes B040 too thin a basis for a prize.

Whether the committee would treat B044 as a trade-shock prize (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) or a broader technology prize, and whether a decade of replication is enough maturity for it. If the committee settled these in B044's favour, my ranking would change.

My assessment draws on the supplied round-1 statements, the chair's summary and general knowledge. I have not independently verified citation counts, attribution details or the firm-level evidence mentioned above.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Kiyotaki or Moore is apparent from my supplied profile. My co-authors (mainly Kaplan, plus Axelson, Weisbach, Jenkinson, Lerner and others) are not credited on B040, B044 or B036. My Chicago Booth adjunct post, KVA vice presidency and Stockholm roles do not link to the preferred or alternative candidates as far as I can tell. I disclose field adjacency: my work on corporate finance and financial contracting overlaps with the collateral and financing-constraint channel, and I chaired the committee for the 2016 contract-theory prize. To my knowledge Moore has also worked on contracts and debt, but my citation rests only on the 1997 collateral-constraint mechanism. I disclose this without adjudicating it and have tried to apply the common criteria. I also note that I am one of four B040 supporters, including the chair, and I do not treat that as merit.
